Postnatal depression is a common and important OSCE topic. You may be asked to take a psychiatric history, interpret the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), assess suicide risk, counsel a mother, or discuss treatment while breastfeeding.
The key OSCE principle is to recognise depression, assess the safety of both mother and baby, and initiate appropriate treatment and follow-up.

subsections.subsection_title: 1. What the OSCE station may say

items.text: History taking: A woman presents six weeks after delivery with persistent sadness, fatigue and loss of interest. Take a focused history.
Screening: Interpret an EPDS questionnaire completed by a postpartum woman.
Risk assessment: A mother says her family would be better off without her. Assess her suicide risk.
Counselling: Explain postnatal depression to a woman who feels guilty about not enjoying motherhood.
Management: Outline treatment options, including psychological therapy and antidepressants.
Breastfeeding: Counsel a mother who needs antidepressant treatment but wishes to continue breastfeeding.
Differential diagnosis: Distinguish postnatal depression from postpartum blues, postpartum psychosis and ordinary postpartum fatigue.

blocks.text: Postnatal depression is a depressive episode occurring after childbirth, characterised by persistent low mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure, together with other depressive symptoms that cause clinically significant distress or impairment.
It may begin during the first few weeks after delivery or develop months later. It can persist if untreated.
Symptoms are not simply the expected tiredness and emotional changes associated with caring for a newborn.

content_groups.group_title: Postnatal depression versus postpartum blues versus postpartum psychosis

blocks.text: Postpartum blues
Usually starts in the first few days and resolves within two weeks. Symptoms include tearfulness, irritability and emotional lability, without persistent severe impairment or psychosis.
Postnatal depression

Persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, hopelessness and impaired daily functioning. Symptoms generally last at least two weeks, although clinical assessment should not be delayed when symptoms are severe.
Postpartum psychosis
Acute psychiatric emergency involving delusions, hallucinations, marked confusion or severe mood disturbance with possible loss of contact with reality.
Exam tip: Postnatal depression can occur without psychosis. However, severe depression may include suicidal thoughts, and psychotic depression requires urgent specialist assessment.

blocks.text: Risk factors help guide assessment but are not diagnostic. Postnatal depression can affect women with no obvious risk factors and can occur after an apparently uncomplicated delivery.
In the OSCE, organise symptoms into mood, cognition, biological symptoms, functioning and safety.
A. Emotional symptoms

items.text: Persistent sadness or tearfulness.
Loss of interest or pleasure.
Hopelessness and helplessness.
Irritability or anxiety.
Feeling overwhelmed by motherhood.
Emotional numbness or detachment.

blocks.text: B. Cognitive symptoms

items.text: Excessive guilt or self-blame.
Feeling like a bad mother.
Poor concentration and indecisiveness.
Worthlessness or hopelessness.
Recurrent thoughts of death or suicide.

blocks.text: C. Biological symptoms

items.text: Insomnia even when the baby is asleep, or excessive sleeping.
Reduced appetite or overeating.
Low energy.
Reduced libido.
Psychomotor slowing or agitation.

blocks.text: D. Functional symptoms

items.text: Difficulty with self-care.
Difficulty completing daily activities.
Difficulty bonding with the baby.
Withdrawal from family and friends.
Difficulty making decisions or managing infant care.

blocks.text: Fatigue, poor sleep and appetite changes may result from normal postpartum recovery. Ask whether symptoms are persistent, disproportionate, associated with low mood or loss of pleasure, and causing significant distress or impairment.
A mother may love her baby and still have postnatal depression. Difficulty bonding does not mean that she does not love her child.

"Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I understand that things have been difficult since your delivery. I would like to talk about your mood, sleep, daily activities and how you have been coping. I will also ask a few questions about your safety, because these are important when someone is feeling low. Everything you share will be treated confidentially, except where we need to take action to protect you or someone else. Is that okay?"

content_groups.group_title: Communication skills expected by the examiner

items.text: Sit at the patient's level and maintain an open posture.
Allow the patient time to speak without interruption.
Use open questions before specific questions.
Validate her feelings without judgement.
Avoid statements such as "You should be happy; you have a beautiful baby."
Explain that postnatal depression is a treatable illness and is not a personal failure.
Ask permission before involving a partner or family member, unless urgent safety circumstances require otherwise.

blocks.text: A strong OSCE history should identify the depressive syndrome, its duration, severity, functional impact, differential diagnoses and immediate risks.

content_groups.group_title: A. Presenting complaint and history of presenting illness

items.text: How have you been feeling since delivery?
When did you first notice the change in your mood?
Has it been present most days?
Have you been feeling sad, empty or hopeless?
Have you lost interest in activities you previously enjoyed?
Do you still enjoy spending time with your baby?
Are there periods when you feel better?
Is the problem getting worse?
Has it affected your relationship or ability to care for yourself?

blocks.text: Establish the duration of symptoms. A depressive episode commonly involves symptoms persisting for at least two weeks, but urgent symptoms should be assessed immediately regardless of duration.

items.text: How many hours do you sleep in 24 hours?
Can you sleep when someone else cares for the baby?
Do you wake early and struggle to return to sleep?
Do you feel exhausted throughout the day?
Do you feel unusually energetic despite very little sleep?

blocks.text: The last question is important because a reduced need for sleep accompanied by increased energy may suggest mania rather than uncomplicated depression.

items.text: Appetite and weight changes.
Energy levels.
Concentration and memory.
Psychomotor slowing or restlessness.
Loss of interest in sex.
Pain, postpartum bleeding or other physical complaints.
Do you blame yourself for things that have happened?
Do you feel you are failing as a mother?
Do you feel connected to your baby?
Do you feel emotionally numb around your baby?
Do you worry that you cannot care for your baby properly?
Have you had unwanted, frightening thoughts about your baby?

blocks.text: If intrusive thoughts are reported, clarify whether they are unwanted and distressing, whether the mother fears acting on them, whether there is intent or a plan, and whether she has delusional beliefs or hallucinations. Intrusive thoughts alone do not establish intent to harm.

content_groups.group_title: E. Suicide and self-harm risk assessment

blocks.text: This is one of the most important parts of the station.

items.text: Have you felt that life is not worth living?
Have you wished that you would not wake up?
Have you thought about harming yourself?
Have you thought about ending your life?
Have you considered how you might do it?
Have you made a plan or taken any steps towards acting on these thoughts?
Do you have access to the means you have considered?
Have you attempted suicide or harmed yourself in the past?
What has stopped you from acting on these thoughts?
Do you feel able to keep yourself and your baby safe today?

blocks.text: Also assess infant safety, thoughts of harming the baby, psychotic symptoms, substance use, available support and protective factors.
If there is current suicidal intent, a plan, inability to maintain safety, or suspected psychosis, arrange urgent emergency assessment. Do not leave the patient unsupported while help is arranged.

blocks.text: Examiner's point: Screen for bipolar disorder before initiating antidepressant monotherapy, particularly if there is a history suggestive of mania or hypomania.

content_groups.group_title: Example of a mental state examination report

blocks.text: "The patient appears tired and tearful, with reduced eye contact and limited spontaneous speech. Her mood is subjectively low, and her affect is constricted. Her thoughts are dominated by guilt and feelings of inadequacy as a mother. No hallucinations or delusions are elicited during this assessment. Her concentration is reduced. Suicide risk requires further assessment, including intent, plans, access to means, previous attempts and protective factors."
Do not document suicidal ideation as absent unless it has actually been assessed.

The EPDS is a 10-item self-report screening questionnaire used to identify women who may need further assessment for depression and related mental health difficulties during pregnancy or after childbirth.
It is a screening tool, not a diagnostic test.

items.text: There are 10 questions.
Each question is scored from 0 to 3.
Total score ranges from 0 to 30.
Higher scores generally indicate greater symptom burden.
Item 10 asks about thoughts of self-harm and requires particular attention.

blocks.text: Thresholds vary by local guideline and service. A commonly used approach is:

rows: Lower symptom burden; assess clinically if concerns remain
Possible depression; assess symptoms and consider support or repeat assessment
Higher likelihood of depression; comprehensive clinical assessment is indicated
Prompt, direct suicide-risk assessment, regardless of total score

blocks.text: These are practical screening bands, not universal diagnostic cut-offs. Some services use a threshold of 10 or higher to trigger further assessment. Always follow the validated local protocol.
A woman six weeks after delivery scores 15 on the EPDS. What would you do?
Model answer:

"This score suggests a significant burden of depressive symptoms and warrants a comprehensive clinical assessment. I would explore symptom duration, severity, functional impairment, suicide and infant-safety risks, and possible bipolar disorder or psychosis. I would then develop an appropriate management plan based on clinical findings rather than relying on the score alone."
**Examiner asks: What if the total score is only 7 but the patient says she wants to die?**
Answer: A low total score does not override a concerning clinical history. I would assess her safety immediately and arrange urgent help according to the findings.

rows: Mild, short-lived emotional lability, usually resolving within two weeks
Delusions, hallucinations, severe mood disturbance or confusion
Depressive episode with a history of mania or hypomania
Excessive worry, fear, physical anxiety symptoms
Intrusive unwanted thoughts and/or compulsions, often with preserved insight
Re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal following trauma
Fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise tolerance and possible low mood
Mood changes with possible weight, temperature tolerance or heart-rate changes

blocks.text: Remember that more than one condition can coexist. For example, a woman can have both postnatal depression and an anxiety disorder.
Postnatal depression is diagnosed clinically. Investigations are selected to identify contributing medical conditions or alternative diagnoses.

rows: Electrolytes, renal function and other chemistry tests
If physical illness, poor intake or medication considerations warrant them
Vitamin B12, folate or other nutritional tests
Identify adverse effects or substance-related symptoms

blocks.text: Additional testing depends on the history and examination. Routine extensive investigations are not necessary for every otherwise well woman.
Management depends on severity, functional impairment, suicide risk, psychiatric history, patient preferences and breastfeeding considerations.

items.text: Assess safety first. Determine suicide and infant-safety risks, screen for psychosis and mania, and assess the woman's ability to care safely for herself and her baby.
Assess severity. Consider symptom duration, daily functioning, previous episodes and available support.
Agree on treatment. Offer psychological therapy, medication when indicated, or both according to severity and clinical history.
Address contributing factors. Support sleep, nutrition, physical recovery, practical childcare and treatment of medical conditions.
Arrange follow-up. Monitor symptoms, functioning, adverse effects, safety and treatment response.

blocks.text: **A. Mild symptoms**

items.text: Guided self-help based on cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT).
Supportive counselling.
Psychoeducation about postnatal depression.
Practical support with infant care and household responsibilities.
Help with sleep opportunities and feeding difficulties.
Planned reassessment to ensure symptoms are improving.

blocks.text: Do not dismiss persistent symptoms as normal adjustment merely because they appear mild.
**B. Moderate depression**

items.text: Individual CBT.
Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT).
An antidepressant when indicated.
A combination of psychological therapy and medication when appropriate.
More frequent review when there are significant symptoms, limited support or safety concerns.

blocks.text: **C. Severe depression**
Severe depression requires prompt specialist assessment, particularly if there is marked functional impairment, inability to care for the infant safely, suicidal intent or psychotic symptoms.

items.text: Urgent psychiatric referral.
Hospital admission if required for safety or treatment.
Antidepressant treatment where appropriate.
Combined psychological and pharmacological treatment.
Specialist treatment for psychotic depression or bipolar disorder when present.
A clear safety and infant-care plan.

blocks.text: If psychosis or mania is suspected, do not treat the presentation as uncomplicated unipolar depression.
Medication decisions should be individualised. Discuss the benefits of treating depression, potential adverse effects, prior treatment response, infant factors and the mother's preferences.

rows: Often a preferred SSRI when initiating treatment during breastfeeding because infant exposure through milk is generally low
An option in selected cases; consider previous response and infant exposure
Effective, but its long half-life and active metabolite can result in greater infant exposure than some alternatives
Selection depends on clinical history, prior response, interactions and lactation guidance

blocks.text: Do not switch an effective medication automatically just because a woman is breastfeeding. The risks of untreated maternal depression must also be considered.

content_groups.group_title: Example counselling for a breastfeeding mother

blocks.text: "Postnatal depression is treatable, and breastfeeding does not automatically prevent us from using medication. We will consider which medicine is most suitable for you and your baby, taking account of your previous treatment and the amount that passes into breast milk. We will also monitor your recovery and look out for any relevant adverse effects in your baby."

items.text: Improvement in mood, sleep, interest and functioning.
Suicidal thoughts or emerging agitation.
Nausea, gastrointestinal symptoms, sleep changes and sexual adverse effects.
Adherence and the patient's concerns about medication.
Symptoms suggesting mania or hypomania.
Infant feeding, alertness and other clinically relevant effects when breastfeeding.

blocks.text: Explain that antidepressants do not usually produce their full benefit immediately. Early review is important, especially when suicide risk or severe symptoms are present.
Important: Avoid abrupt discontinuation of antidepressants without clinical advice. Medication should be reviewed with the treating clinician.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Counselling a woman with postnatal depression

blocks.text: You are asked to counsel a 28-year-old woman six weeks after delivery. She says:
"I cry every day. I don't enjoy anything anymore, and I feel like a terrible mother because I don't feel happy around my baby."
Step 1: Acknowledge her distress
"I'm sorry that things have been so difficult. Thank you for telling me how you feel."
Step 2: Explain the condition
"What you are describing may be postnatal depression. This can happen after childbirth and can affect mood, sleep, energy, confidence and how you experience everyday activities."
Step 3: Reassure without minimising
"This does not mean you are a bad mother, and it is not your fault. Many women experience this, and effective treatments are available."
Step 4: Assess safety
"When people feel as low as you have described, they sometimes have thoughts of harming themselves or feel that life is not worth living. Have you experienced anything like that?"
Ask separately about thoughts of harming the baby, intent, plans, psychotic symptoms and her ability to keep herself and the baby safe.
Step 5: Explain treatment options

"Treatment may involve talking therapy, medication or both, depending on how severe the symptoms are. We will decide together what is appropriate for you, including any considerations relating to breastfeeding."
Step 6: Discuss practical support

"It may help to have someone you trust assist with household tasks and baby care so you can rest and attend appointments. We can also discuss feeding difficulties, sleep and other pressures contributing to how you feel."
Step 7: Agree on follow-up
Explain when and how you will review her symptoms, who to contact if she worsens, and where to obtain urgent help.
The partner or family may believe the mother is ungrateful, lazy or unwilling to care for the baby. Address this without blame.

items.text: Depression is a treatable illness, not a character defect.
Criticism and pressure to "be happy" can increase shame and isolation.
Practical support with feeding, childcare and household tasks can help.
The mother should be encouraged to attend treatment and follow-up.
Family members should take suicidal statements, severe deterioration or unusual beliefs seriously.
The family should seek urgent help if the mother cannot keep herself or the baby safe.

blocks.text: Ask the woman whom she wants involved in her care and respect her confidentiality, subject to relevant safety obligations.

subsections.subsection_title: 15. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the difference between postpartum blues and postnatal depression?

Postpartum blues are common, mild emotional changes that usually resolve within two weeks. Postnatal depression involves more persistent depressive symptoms, often lasting at least two weeks, with clinically significant distress or impairment.
Q2. Can postnatal depression occur without risk factors?
Yes. Risk factors increase the likelihood but are not required for diagnosis.
Q3. What is the EPDS?
The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is a 10-item screening questionnaire used to identify women who may need further assessment for perinatal depression and related symptoms.
Q4. Does an EPDS score confirm depression?
No. It is a screening tool. Diagnosis requires clinical assessment, including symptom duration, severity, functional impact and differential diagnoses.
Q5. What must you assess before prescribing an antidepressant?
Suicide risk, symptom severity, bipolar disorder or mania, psychosis, current medications, previous treatment response, medical history, breastfeeding considerations and the patient's preferences.
Q6. Which antidepressant is commonly considered when initiating treatment in a breastfeeding woman?
Sertraline is often a preferred option because infant exposure through breast milk is generally low. The final choice depends on individual circumstances and previous response.
Q7. Should a woman stop breastfeeding because she has postnatal depression?
No. Depression alone is not a reason to stop breastfeeding. Support feeding according to the mother's wishes and clinical circumstances, and assess the safety of any prescribed medication.
Q8. When is urgent psychiatric referral required?
Examples include suicidal intent or plans, inability to maintain safety, suspected postpartum psychosis, mania, severe functional impairment, or concerns that the baby cannot be cared for safely.
Q9. How would you manage a mother who reports thoughts of harming her baby?

Clarify whether the thoughts are unwanted and intrusive or involve intent, plans, delusions or hallucinations. Assess immediate risk, arrange appropriate supervision and infant care, and obtain urgent specialist assessment when safety is in doubt.
Q10. What if symptoms do not improve with treatment?

Review the diagnosis, adherence, dose and duration of treatment, adverse effects, psychosocial stressors, comorbidities and possible bipolar disorder. Consider specialist referral and an alternative or combined treatment plan.
Q11. Can postnatal depression affect bonding?
Yes. Depression may make it difficult to feel emotionally connected to the baby, but this does not mean the mother does not love the child. Support and effective treatment can help.
Q12. How can recurrence be prevented?

Identify previous episodes, develop a plan for future pregnancies and postpartum periods, review medication with a clinician, establish early symptom monitoring, support sleep and arrange timely follow-up.

items.text: Attributing persistent depression to normal postpartum adjustment.
Failing to ask about suicide directly.
Assuming a low EPDS score excludes serious illness.
Failing to assess for mania or bipolar disorder.
Treating intrusive thoughts as proof of intent without clarifying their nature.
Automatically stopping breastfeeding or withholding treatment.
Prescribing antidepressants without reviewing relevant medical and psychiatric history.
Failing to discuss practical support and follow-up.
Providing reassurance without assessing safety.
Discharging a high-risk patient without an appropriate safety plan.

subsections.subsection_title: 18. Example of a complete OSCE presentation

blocks.text: The examiner asks you to summarise a woman who presents six weeks after childbirth with persistent sadness, loss of interest, poor sleep, guilt and difficulty bonding with her baby.
Model presentation:

"This is a woman six weeks postpartum presenting with persistent low mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, guilt and impaired functioning. The history is suggestive of postnatal depression. I would establish symptom duration and severity, assess suicide and infant-safety risks, screen for bipolar disorder and psychosis, and review obstetric, medical, psychiatric and psychosocial factors. I would perform a focused mental state and physical examination, request investigations guided by the clinical findings, and develop a management plan involving psychological therapy and, if indicated, antidepressant treatment. I would consider breastfeeding, arrange appropriate follow-up and provide clear instructions for obtaining urgent help if symptoms worsen."
